title: Money Stuff: Anthropic Has Some Anchor Investors
contentHtml:
Happy Anthropic IPO day

You know the basic theory of AI circular financing, right? It’s:

  1. If you give Anthropic PBC a certain amount of money — say $74 — you get a share of Anthropic stock. This gives you partial ownership of Anthropic’s future profits. If those profits are high, the stock will go up and you will make money.
  2. If Google gives Anthropic the same amount of money ($74), it gets a share of Anthropic stock, and if the stock goes up Google will make money. But Google also gets something else. Anthropic has agreed to pay Google something like $250 billion for computing capacity over the next seven years.[1] Anthropic does not currently have $250 billion, although it is increasingly cash-flow positive, and it is not exactly an investment-grade credit. The more money Anthropic has, the better its chances of actually paying Google that $250 billion. In some loose sense, the money that Google gives Anthropic for stock comes back to Google as revenue. Plus it gets the stock.

For “Google” you could substitute “Nvidia” or “Broadcom” or “AMD” or “TSMC” or a number of other giant providers of picks and shovels to the artificial intelligence industry.

One conclusion you could take away from this is, like, ooh the AI industry is a house of cards, ooh the revenue is all fake, ooh, ooh. That’s definitely a conclusion that people draw, but it doesn’t seem especially compelled by this description, and I am not going to spend any time on it.

Another conclusion you could take away, though, is just that Anthropic stock is worth more to Google than it is to you. Every dollar that Google invests in Anthropic gets it (1) some Anthropic stock and (2) some revenue; every dollar that you invest in Anthropic gets you just the Anthropic stock. Google’s package is more valuable than your package.

I almost added “… so Google should pay more for it,” but that doesn’t strictly follow. Arguably a dollar from Google is worth more to Anthropic than a dollar from you, if Google’s dollar comes with an implicit or explicit promise of providing compute or chips or other inputs that Anthropic needs. Google putting money into Anthropic arguably creates value, which Google and Anthropic can split, in a way that you putting money into Anthropic doesn’t. Arguably Google should be willing to pay more for an Anthropic share than you are, but Anthropic should be willing to sell Google a share for less than it charges you.

We talked about this back in 2024, when venture capitalist Apoorv Agrawal pointed it out as a problem for venture capitalists:

As MANG [Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Nvidia] sets prices on these rounds (e.g. OpenAI by MSFT), what does the valuation represent?

Does it make sense for a financial investor to participate in these rounds?

If a $1 investment by Google or Nvidia gets them $1 of revenue and $1 of stock, then the stock can’t really be worth $1, can it? If you’re just some venture capitalist investing in the same round at the same valuation, aren’t you overpaying?

A fun question for venture capitalists in 2024. But in 2026, Anthropic is launching its initial public offering. It filed a revised prospectus this morning, offering 825 million shares at a range of $70 to $78 per share. It has not been the best, like, two-week period in the history of AI financing. For a while, there was talk of a $2 trillion valuation in the IPO, but the target has come down. Bloomberg’s Bailey Lipschultz reports:

Anthropic PBC is seeking a valuation of about $1.4 trillion in its initial public offering, in a bid to make history as the first frontier artificial intelligence lab to go public.

The Claude chatbot maker and its co-founders are seeking to raise as much as $90.4 billion in the IPO and a private placement. The base offering would raise up to $64.4 billion, with shares marketed for $70 to $78 each, according to a filing on Tuesday with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Anthropic is offering 801.4 million shares, while [its co-founders] are selling 23.6 million shares. …

At the top of the price range, Anthropic would have a market value of about $1 trillion, based on the shares outstanding listed in the filing. Accounting for employee stock options, restricted shares and stock reserved for the company’s charitable donation matching program, Anthropic would have a fully diluted value of about $1.4 trillion. ...

The goal defies jitters from a sharp selloff in AI-related stocks last week, driven by expectations that politicians promising tougher regulation of data centers and related infrastructure will drive up costs and limit development of the technology.

One thing that helps is that, of the $90 billion target, $26 billion will come in a private placement to strategic investors. Anthropic says:

We have entered into an agreement with each of Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC, … Micron Technology, Inc., Microsoft Corporation, NVIDIA Corporation, and TSMC Partners, Ltd., pursuant to which they have agreed, severally and not jointly, to purchase an aggregate of $26.0 billion of our Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the initial public offering price.

This has several nice features for Anthropic:

  • No fees. Anthropic will probably pay its underwriters fees in the ballpark of 1% of the $60 billion or so that it targets raising in the IPO,[2] but it will pay them $0 for the $26 billion that it raises from Google, Nvidia and friends. (“The underwriters will not receive any underwriting discounts or commissions on the shares of Class N common stock sold in the concurrent private placement.“) Presumably the banks are doing some work on the private placement, but the main thing that Anthropic is paying its IPO underwriters for is finding investors, and the underwriters didn’t find these investors. These investors know Anthropic well.
  • No votes. Regular investors in the IPO get Class A shares, which have one vote per share. We talked last month about Anthropic’s menagerie of share classes, and the short version is that regular Class A investors don’t get all that much of a say over how Anthropic is run; its founders and employees and various councils of wise elders pretty much control the company. But the strategic investors in the private placement get Class N shares, which have even less control; they have zero votes per share. “Amazon and Google rank below the regular shareholders,” I wrote, “presumably to reflect their connection to filthy commerce.” AMD, Broadcom, Google, etc. all have commercial interests — in having Anthropic pay them a lot for chips — that might diverge from the interests of Anthropic shareholders more broadly, and Anthropic insulates itself from conflict by not letting them vote.[3] Plus nonvoting shares make the antitrust analysis easier.
  • No flipping. Regular investors who buy in the IPO can immediately resell their shares, but the strategic investors in the private placement are locked up for a bit. (They are not technically subject to lockup agreements, but their shares are not registered and can’t practically be sold on the stock exchange for about six months.[4]) This constrains the supply of shares available on the stock exchange, and perhaps keeps the price up.
  • No price sensitivity: Google and friends have committed to buy $26 billion worth of stock at whatever price the IPO clears at. They do not have to be picky about valuation. For one thing, most IPOs go up, and with modern technology surely Anthropic can price its IPO for a nice pop when it opens for trading. The strategic private investors can simply trust Anthropic, its bankers and the public investors to figure out the right IPO price. For another thing, though, arguably a share of Anthropic is worth a bit more to Google and friends than it is to the rest of the IPO investors, so they will be happy at whatever price the IPO investors agree to.

I don’t want to overstate this: “Anthropic stock is worth more to Google than to you” becomes less true as Anthropic gets bigger and makes more money. The $26 billion that the strategic investors are putting in here is pretty small relative to Anthropic’s future compute needs.

Still, if you can sell a quarter of your IPO to price-insensitive long-term investors with no fees, that is just a good deal. Anyway the IPO kicked off marketing this morning and is scheduled to price next week, and Lipschultz reported:

The IPO was fully covered with orders from prospective investors for all the available shares when the deal launched, according to people familiar with the matter.

I assume they spend the rest of the roadshow working the valuation up to $2 trillion.[5]

S\

Sorry but I have to talk about maybe the dumbest thing I have ever seen in equity capital markets. On June 1, 2026, Anthropic PBC filed a confidential first draft of the prospectus for its initial public offering. On Sept. 29, 2026, President Donald Trump issued an executive order saying that from now on “artificial intelligence” (AI) should be called “super intelligence” (SI). Everyone had a good laugh. On Oct. 26, almost a month after the executive order, Anthropic filed the first public draft of that prospectus; it filed a revised draft the following week. Like everyone else in the AI business except Elon Musk, Anthropic called AI AI in its prospectus. It used the term “SI,” but for something else: “‘SIs’ refer to systems integrators, or third-party technology and professional services firms that design, build, and deploy integrated solutions for customers,” etc. The defined term for what Anthropic does is: “‘AI’ refers to artificial intelligence, a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual environments.”

Today, as Anthropic kicks off the marketing for its IPO, it filed an amended draft of the prospectus. Apparently somebody — at the US Securities and Exchange Commission? at the White House? — sat Anthropic down and was like “no he really means this SI thing.” And so the revised draft prospectus:

  1. No longer abbreviates “systems integrator” as “SI.”
  2. Has a new defined term for “‘super intelligence’ or ‘SI,’” defined the same way as AI was previously.
  3. Keeps the same definition of “artificial intelligence,” and says that “for purposes of this prospectus, to avoid confusion, we use the terms ‘super intelligence,’ ‘SI,’ ‘artificial intelligence,’ and ‘AI’ interchangeably.” I do not see how that would avoid confusion!
  4. Sort of halfheartedly does a search-and-replace for some but not all of the occurrences of “AI.”

So the cover page, and the non-searchable image of the letter from the founders, still use “AI.” But then the “overview” of Anthropic on page 6 begins (emphasis added):

For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason, analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this abundance of super intelligence will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. …

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define SI. We are first and foremost a research lab — our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.

And then most of the references in the body of the prospectus are to “super intelligence,” not “artificial intelligence,” though there are some slips. (It calls Claude a “new type of artificially intelligent entity,” either because nobody Ctrl-F’ed “artificially intelligent” or because calling Claude a “new type of super intelligent entity” was too obviously gibberish.) On the other hand, most of the abbreviated references are to “AI,” though a few dozen are to “SI.”

Does this matter? No. But, like … intelligence!? Here is a company whose pitch is that it will create a new superintelligent god, a “country of geniuses in a datacenter,” that can usher in an age of miracles and solve any problem facing mankind. And faced with the practical stupid problem of “hey the president wants us to call our product SI instead of AI, but we already mentioned AI hundreds of times in our prospectus,” Anthropic and its team of highly paid advisers were like “well we’d better have a first-year associate search for ‘AI’ and replace it with ‘SI,’ that will probably have an error rate of no more than 50%.” And, fine, fair, if it’s not worth doing at all, then it’s not worth doing well. But they didn’t do it well!

Also Anthropic has a very cool logo, “A\,” like the first letter of its name (A) followed by a backslash that presumably represents an “I,” for “artificial intelligence,” a nice visual motif that doesn’t work if you’re going around pretending that your product is called “SI.” Should have renamed the company Santhropic.[6] Ugh.

Also: Anthropic apparently sent out, and then retracted, the wrong version of its prospectus yesterday.

Regime change

The most important thing to understand in global financial markets for about 40 years, from the early 1980s to the early 2020s, was “interest rates go down.” Many, many huge financial stories — celebrity bond managers, the rise of private equity, various tech booms, crypto, etc. — were basically epiphenomena on the fact that rates went down. This was not a law of nature, as far as I know. Rates could go up. But, for 40 years, they mostly didn’t. Sometimes they did! But then they went back down again. The trend was your friend.

This might still be true in the long run, and in 2028 interest rates might be zero; it is hard to know the role of interest rates in a post-artificial-general-intelligence world. But, for about the last five years, rates have gone up. It is not the case that every piece of financial news in the last five years is an epiphenomenon on “people forgot that rates could go up but then they did” — surely AI isn’t?[7] — but a lot of them are. Bloomberg’s Michelle Amponsah, Prashant Gopal and Paulina Cachero report that, for a long time in the 2020s, real estate agents and mortgage brokers and consumers made financial decisions based on the assumption that rates always go down, but then instead rates went up:

Buying a home in the last few years has meant hearing the same refrain: “Marry the house, date the rate.”

The idea, boosted by Realtors, mortgage bankers and influencers as interest rates started rising in 2022, was that buyers shouldn’t worry too much about loan costs. Focus instead on getting the house you want, then refinance when rates inevitably came down.

For a generation of buyers conditioned to cheap mortgages — with rates reaching historic lows during the pandemic — it was easy to embrace the idea. But the promise behind that slogan has yet to materialize.

Economists had forecast that this would be the year mortgage rates finally came back down to Earth, continuing the four-decade trend of falling rates. Instead, they’ve climbed above 7% and show little sign of retreating. For the more than 11 million borrowers locked into mortgage rates of 6% or more, the bet on “dating” a rate has become a costly long-term relationship.

Right, right, “interest rates always go down” was, in 2022, pretty well grounded in empirical data. You can sort of see why everyone believed it.

Oh Jensen

As we discussed yesterday:

  1. It came out over the weekend that Jensen Huang, the chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
  2. People had previously speculated that Huang might be having an affair with a Chinese spy, but Huang and Nvidia had denied it, calling their relationship “normal.”
  3. This is bad for Nvidia for an assortment of obvious reasons. Huang is essential to Nvidia’s success and the company has no real succession plan, so it would be bad to lose him, and the scandal might lead to more restrictions on Nvidia’s sale of chips abroad.
  4. So the news wiped about $200 billion off of Nvidia’s stock value yesterday.
  5. “If a CEO has an affair that knocks hundreds of billions of dollars off the stock price,” I wrote, “shareholder plaintiffs’ lawyers are going to demand a cut.”

By last night, the first lawsuit had been filed. Here it is:

Defendants made false and/or misleading statements and/or failed to disclose that: (1) Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, who also has a role at a company called Megaspeed, which is suspected of helping China evade export controls; (2) as such, Nvidia’s statements about its relationship with Megaspeed were materially false and misleading at all relevant times; (3) the foregoing raised concerns in the national security community about Nvidia and, if revealed, presented a material risk to the Company’s reputation and business prospects; and (4) as a result, Defendants’ public statements were materially false and/or misleading at all relevant times. …

As a result of Defendants’ wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company’s securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages.

Etc. I don’t know that the extreme efficiency of the Everything-Is-Securities-Fraud machine actually makes, like, companies or capital markets any better. Presumably in a counterfactual world in which lawyers did not immediately bring securities fraud lawsuits like this, Nvidia’s board of directors would still have incentives to discourage its CEO from having affairs with Chinese spies, although in that world as in this one the heart wants what it wants and sometimes that’s a Chinese spy.

But in any case, in our actual world, the very most predictable fact about the US legal and financial system is that if the CEO of a multitrillion-dollar company has an affair with a Chinese spy, there are going to be securities fraud lawsuits.

Things happen

Anthropic Plans IPO Live Stream With Amodei, JPMorgan CEO Dimon. Anthropic Unveils New Fable, Mythos AI Models Ahead of IPO. Wall Street Bonuses Projected to Climb Before Prospects Weaken. Goldman, Capital Group Alumni Debut AI-Run Stock-Picking Fund. Mercedes Gives Its Cars an AI Upgrade. Trump Media Posts First-Ever Profit as Crypto Boosts Results. Singapore seizes ‘forever’ cruise ship that dumped passengers in Cambodia. The Parents Suing Schools Because Their Kids Got Bad Grades. The sports gambling spiral.

[1] See page 179 of the Anthropic prospectus: “In March 2026, we entered into a CSP hosting agreement with Google, which was subsequently amended between May and October 2026, pursuant to which we committed to spend at least approximately $121.3 billion between April 2026 and July 2033, regardless of actual usage. ... In addition, we also committed to procure additional TPU compute, without a fixed dollar commitment, via one of various delivery methods, including either a CSP hosting agreement with Google, direct purchase from Google with five-year financing, or direct purchase and/or lease from a third-party TPU provider with five-year financing. ... We estimate the aggregate future payments for such additional compute to be approximately $125.0 billion to $150.0 billion, which are not included in the contractual obligations table above.”

[2] The fees are not yet disclosed in the prospectus, but page 127 gives some clues. “Each $1.00 increase or decrease in the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set forth on the cover page of this prospectus, would increase or decrease, as applicable, the net proceeds that we receive from this offering and the concurrent private placement by approximately $793 million,” it says. Anthropic is offering 801,351,354 shares in the primary offering, so a $1 price increase would increase *gross* proceeds by $801.4 million. (The proceeds of the private placement are unaffected: It’s $26 billion regardless of price.) The difference is about $8.4 million, or about 1.04%, but of course that $793 million number is rounded and my best guess is the fee is 1%. The total fees and expenses of the base offering seem to be about $700 million, which is, like, a 1% underwriting fee plus legal costs, flights, etc.

[3] When Agrawal complained about strategic circular venture capital investments in 2024, he was worried about valuation but also governance, saying: “MANG aren’t purely financial investors and will have strategic directives that may be misaligned with other purely financial investors. They may limit/block acquisition offers and financing rounds that would have been advantageous from a financial standpoint but didn’t align with their strategic interests.” The nonvoting shares helps address that concern.

[4] See page 320: “The shares of Class N common stock sold in the concurrent private placement will not be subject to the lock-up agreements or market standoff agreements described above. These shares will be ‘restricted securities’ within the meaning of Rule 144 and may not be resold absent registration under the Securities Act or an available exemption from registration. ... In general, once we have been subject to the reporting requirements of Section 13 or Section 15(d) of the Exchange Act for at least 90 days, a purchaser that is not our affiliate may resell such shares under Rule 144 after holding them for at least six months, and a purchaser that is our affiliate remains subject to the volume, manner of sale, and notice conditions of Rule 144 described below.” Google has some registration rights for its stock, though.

[5] For what it’s worth, it’s around $1.7 trillion on Hyperliquid.

[6] Or, like, ’Santhropic, short for Misanthropic.

[7] I know, you’re gonna email. Go ahead. “The AI boom is the result of interest rates going up”: Discuss.
